summary_plain: This ground-based investigation studied how flames spread across solid materials in microgravity to improve spacecraft fire safety. Researchers used advanced computer models and compared them with images from previous space experiments. Understanding these burning behaviors helps engineers design safer materials and prevent fires during space missions.
summary_expert: This ground-based investigation developed and validated unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. The approach combined computational fluid-solid response simulations for charring and ablation materials with experimental validation using BASS and BASS-II data. The study evaluated flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate across various sample geometries including flat sheets, spheres, rod-shaped PMMA samples, and wax cylinders. The documents provided describe the objectives and design only.

key_findings.text: The unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) approach was hypothesized to accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including the Goldilocks flammability zone, by coupling near-wall thermal, mass transport, and chemical processes with far-field flow dynamics.

The research approach combined high-resolution computational modeling with experimental validation using two-color tomography methods applied to DSLR camera imagery from BASS and BASS-II investigations.
Evaluation metrics for comparing model predictions to experiments included flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate.

earth_applications: Improving combustion modeling by deepening our understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes
Enabling more effective fire prevention and mitigation strategies
Fostering innovations in diagnostics and simulations applicable across a variety of combustion scenarios
